Part D · Chapter 4

Self-attention

How a token gets a weighted blend of information from itself and earlier tokens

In a model such as GPT-2, self-attention is the step in which a token gets a weighted blend of information from itself and the tokens before it. This chapter builds the step from a four-token example with made-up vectors, then adds the scaling, the causal mask and many heads. The attention weights of GPT-2 small on three sentences written for this primer were computed beforehand, outside your browser.

You will need: the dot product and matrix products with transposes (0.5), softmax and variance (0.7), tokens (D1), embeddings (D2) and the context window (D3).

What a token needs from the others

Guess first. In “Tag 4127 is a young bamboo shark. We put it back and wrote down Tag 4127.”, the writer reaches the second “Tag” and is about to write the number again. Which earlier token would help a model most to guess the next one: “young”, “We” or “▁4” (a space and the digit 4, the first piece of 4127)? Why?

Attention is a step in which a model computes, for a token, a weighted blend of information from the tokens of a text. A token reads another token when the model gives the other token an attention weight, a number from 0 to 1. The weights of one token add up to 1. In self-attention the tokens of one text read one another, and in GPT-2 a token reads only itself and the tokens before it. A head is one complete attention computation, and GPT-2 small has 12 heads per layer.

  1. The second ▁Tag (position 16) is selected. Coral lines run to the earlier tokens it reads, thicker for more weight, and the bars give the weights. Later tokens are faded.
  2. In the menu choose another head (L5H5 means layer 5, head 5, counting from 0). At position 16, L4H11 reads the previous token, L0H1 itself, and L1H10 many earlier tokens.

In head L5H5 the second ▁Tag puts 94% of its weight on ▁4, the token that followed the first Tag. The weights are from GPT-2 small, computed beforehand. Most other tokens in this head put their weight on the first token.

How it works

Take the second ▁Tag in head L5H5. Of the 17 tokens it can read, itself included, ▁4 gets 0.94 of the weight and the first token, Tag, gets 0.06. The unrounded weights are 0.942 and 0.056, which leaves 0.002 for the other 15 tokens together. Since ▁4 followed the first Tag, ▁4 is the likely answer to the guess, and reading it can help the model to write the number again.

sumof the weights of the second ▁Tag=0.94weight on ▁4+0.06weight on the first token, Tag+0.00the other 15 tokens together: under 0.01=1the weights add up to 1

Common belief. A large attention weight on a token shows that the token explains the model's output.

Why it fails. A weight says how much one head reads from a token at one step, so it does not show what later layers do with that head's output. Many large weights also go to the first token, which does not identify any part of the sentence.

Better account. The weights describe one step of the computation. To find out what a model used, change the input or the head and watch the output (attention maps as explanations).

Quick quiz

A token at position 3 gives the positions 0, 1 and 2 the weights 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3. What weight does it give itself, and why does position 4 get none?

The four weights add up to 1, so it gives itself 1 − 0.6 = 0.4. In GPT-2 a token reads only itself and the tokens before it, so position 4, a later token, gets no weight.

A friend says: “The weight 0.94 on ▁4 proves that ▁4 explains the next token.” What would you answer, and how would you test the claim?

A weight describes one head at one step, and later layers use the output of the head, so it does not prove an explanation. To test the claim, change the input (for example replace ▁4) or switch off the head, and watch the output.

Sources of the figures

The sentences are written for this primer, and the vectors in the small examples of the next sections are made up. The idea is from Vaswani and others (2017). The figures follow the spirit of Jay Alammar's Illustrated Transformer and of the attention chapter in Grant Sanderson's 3Blue1Brown series.

Reading the figure

The mark ▁ means a space before the token, as in the tokenisation chapter. Select a token by clicking it or with the buttons “Earlier token” and “Later token”. Later tokens are faded because the selected token cannot read them (the causal mask). In the sentence “Tag 4127 twice”, head L5H5 puts its largest weight on the first token for 16 of the 19 tokens that follow it. The exceptions are the three tokens of the repeated Tag 4127. L4H11 looks at the token just before, L0H1 mostly at the token itself, and L1H10 spreads its weight over many earlier tokens, with the most on the nearest ones. The status line under the plot says that these descriptions tell where the weights go on the sentence and do not say what a head is for.

Attention weights and explanation

Jain and Wallace (2019) found that attention weights often do not match other measures of which inputs matter. Wiegreffe and Pinter (2019) replied that the answer depends on what one means by explanation.

The first token and attention sinks

In many heads the first token gets a large share of the weight. The grid in the last section counts 29 heads that put more than 80% of their weight on it, on average over seven short texts. A likely reason is that the weights of a token must add up to 1, so a head with no good match still has to put its weight somewhere. Xiao and others (2024) report that models place such weight on the first tokens, and they call these tokens attention sinks.

An induction head

L5H5 has exceptions to its first-token pattern. When a token, or the same word, has appeared before, the head reads the token that came after the earlier copy. The second ▁Tag and the first Tag are different tokens, because only the second has a leading space. For ▁4 that token is 127, with 0.80 of the weight, and for 127 it is ▁is, with 0.93.

Olsson and others (2022) describe an induction head in two parts. It attends to the token that followed an earlier copy of the current token, and its output makes that token more likely. We tested only the first part, and the test is our own. We drew 20 random sequences of 40 tokens and placed two copies of a sequence one after the other. For the tokens of the second copy, we averaged the weight on the token that followed the earlier copy of the same token. L5H5 gets an average of 0.93, and the other three heads of this chapter get 0.00 to 0.01. So L5H5 matches the first part of the pattern of an induction head. We did not test the second part, and we did not remove the head to see what changes. Such a head could help a model repeat a tag number it has seen.

Queries, keys and values

Guess first. A token has one vector, its embedding. Attention uses a token in three ways: to say what it looks for, to offer a label that other tokens can match, and to hand over its content. Should one vector do all three jobs, or should the model make three different vectors from it?

A projection is a vector made by multiplying another vector with a matrix whose numbers are set by training. From the embedding \(\mathbf{x}\) of a token the model makes three projections, with three matrices \(W_Q\), \(W_K\) and \(W_V\). The query \(\mathbf{q} = W_Q\mathbf{x}\) is what the token looks for, like a search term, and the key \(\mathbf{k} = W_K\mathbf{x}\) is a label that queries are compared with, like the label on a folder. The value \(\mathbf{v} = W_V\mathbf{x}\) is what the token hands over when it is read, like the content of the folder, so the output of attention is built from values.

  1. Choose a token and a role. The boxes show the working: the two numbers of \(\mathbf{q}\) are dot products of the rows of \(W_Q\) with \(\mathbf{x}\). For “it”, \(\mathbf{x} = (1, -0.5, 1)\) gives \(\mathbf{q} = (2, -0.5)\).
  2. Drag the slider x2 from −0.5 to 0.5: q2 becomes 0.5 and q1 stays 2. Switch to Key and Value to see that x2 moves only k1 but moves both v1 and v2.

In this example one embedding gives three different vectors, and changing any number of \(\mathbf{x}\) changes \(\mathbf{q}\), \(\mathbf{k}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\). All numbers are made up.

How it works

Take “it” with \(\mathbf{x} = (1, -0.5, 1)\). The first number of \(\mathbf{q}\) is the dot product of the first row of \(W_Q\), \((1, 0, 1)\), with \(\mathbf{x}\): \(1\times1 + 0\times(-0.5) + 1\times1 = 2\). The second number is \(0\times1 + 1\times(-0.5) + 0\times1 = -0.5\), so \(\mathbf{q} = (2, -0.5)\).

\(\mathbf{q}\)query of “it”: (2, −0.5)=\(W_Q\)rows (1, 0, 1) and (0, 1, 0)×\(\mathbf{x}\)embedding: (1, −0.5, 1)

The embedding itself would do the three jobs poorly. As query, key and value, it would tend to make a token look for tokens with embeddings like its own, because its query would be its own embedding. Its score for another token would then equal that token's score for it. Three separate matrices let training set other comparisons, such as the question “which earlier word names an animal?” asked by “it”. They also let a token offer a content \(\mathbf{v}\) that differs from its label \(\mathbf{k}\).

Where the folder analogy breaks. Nobody writes the labels. Training adjusts \(W_Q\), \(W_K\) and \(W_V\) to improve the predictions, so a key is whatever helps queries find useful tokens, and it may have no neat name. A paper folder keeps the same label, whereas the model computes a new key and a new value for a token in all layers.

Quick quiz

A token has \(\mathbf{x} = (2, 1, 0)\), and the key matrix \(W_K\) has the rows \((0, 1, 0)\) and \((1, 0, -1)\). What is \(\mathbf{k}\)?

The first number is \(0\times2 + 1\times1 + 0\times0 = 1\). The second is \(1\times2 + 0\times1 + (-1)\times0 = 2\). So \(\mathbf{k} = (1, 2)\).

Why does a token need a key and a value as two separate vectors?

The key is used only to compute weights, by comparison with queries. The value is what gets blended into the output. A token can be easy to find and still offer something that differs from its label.

Go deeper why three matrices, GPT-2 sizes, a debug tip about 2 min

Reading the figure

The boxes show the working for the token and the role you choose, and the status line under the plot gives the matrix of that role. The table lists all four tokens, so you can see that one set of matrices gives different \(\mathbf{q}\), \(\mathbf{k}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) to different tokens. Dot products with a row of the matrix are as in the dot product of Part 0. A projection is a matrix product as in the matrices of Part 0.

Why not use the embedding itself?

Then a token's score with itself would be \(\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{x}\), the squared length of \(\mathbf{x}\), and its score with another token could not exceed the product of the two lengths. A token would tend to favour itself and tokens whose vectors are like its own. It could not ask a question such as “which earlier word names an animal?”, because its query would be its own embedding. Separate matrices make the question, the label and the content three different vectors.

In GPT-2 small

The number of entries in \(\mathbf{q}\) and \(\mathbf{k}\) is the key size \(d_k\), here 2. In GPT-2 small the embedding has 768 numbers, a head uses \(\mathbf{q}\), \(\mathbf{k}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) of 64 numbers (\(d_k = 64\)), and 12 heads run side by side (section 6). In the GPT-2 weights used for this chapter, the matrices of a layer are stored as one block of 768 rows and 2,304 columns, since \(3 \times 12 \times 64 = 2{,}304\). Training adjusts these matrices like other parameters, with gradients from backpropagation (B4).

In the first layer the vector \(\mathbf{x}\) that is projected is the token embedding plus a position embedding. In a later layer it is the output of the layer before. In both cases a normalisation step comes first (D5).

Common mistakes

Debug tip. The dot product \(\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k}\) needs \(\mathbf{q}\) and \(\mathbf{k}\) of the same length \(d_k\). The value \(\mathbf{v}\) may have another length \(d_v\), and the output has the length of \(\mathbf{v}\). When a matrix product fails with a size error, print the sizes of all three first.

More questions

A token has \(\mathbf{x} = (1, 0.5, 1)\) and \(W_Q\) has the rows \((1, 0, 1)\) and \((0, 1, 0)\). What is \(\mathbf{q}\)?

The first number is \(1\times 1 + 0 \times 0.5 + 1 \times 1 = 2\). The second is \(0 + 0.5 + 0 = 0.5\). So \(\mathbf{q} = (2, 0.5)\).

Scores, softmax and the weighted sum

Guess first. The token “it” has a query. Its dot products with the keys of “the”, “young”, “hammerhead” and “it” are 0.11, 1.41, 1.98 and 0.80. About what share of its weight goes to “hammerhead”: 25%, 40% or 70%?

The query of a token is compared with the keys of the tokens it reads. The score \(s\) of a pair is the dot product of the query and the key, divided by \(\sqrt{d_k}\). Here \(d_k\), the key size, is the number of entries in the query and in the key. Softmax turns the scores of one query into attention weights, positive numbers that add up to 1, so a larger score gives a larger weight. The output \(\mathbf{o}\) of the token is the weighted sum of the values \(\mathbf{v}\) of the tokens it reads: the values are multiplied by their weights and added.

  1. The coral arrow is the query of “it” and the navy arrows are the keys. The table turns the dot products 0.11, 1.41, 1.98 and 0.80 into the weights 11%, 28%, 42% and 18%; click a row for its working.
  2. Drag the coral tip up and left, to (0.4, 1.0): the weight of “young” becomes larger than that of “hammerhead” (34% against 33%) and the output arrow follows.

Queries and keys: drag the tips

Values: the output is their blend

Moving the query of “it” toward the key of “young” moves weight from “hammerhead” to “young”, and the output follows the values. All vectors are made up.

How it works

Take the row of “hammerhead” in the table, where the query is \((1.2, 0.5)\) and the key is \((1.4, 0.6)\). Their dot product is \(1.2\times1.4 + 0.5\times0.6 = 1.98\), and dividing by \(\sqrt{2} = 1.41\) gives the score 1.40. The four scores 0.08, 1.00, 1.40 and 0.57 give \(e^s\) = 1.08, 2.71, 4.06 and 1.76. These add up to 9.61, so the weight of “hammerhead” is \(4.06 \div 9.61 = 42\%\) and the answer to the guess is about 40%.

\[ s_{ij} = \frac{\mathbf{q}_i\cdot\mathbf{k}_j}{\sqrt{d_k}},\qquad a_{ij} = \frac{e^{s_{ij}}}{\sum_{j'\le i} e^{s_{ij'}}},\qquad \mathbf{o}_i = \sum_{j\le i} a_{ij}\,\mathbf{v}_j \]

Here \(s_{ij}\) is the score of the reading token \(i\) for token \(j\), and \(a_{ij}\) is the weight that \(i\) gives to \(j\). The vector \(\mathbf{o}_i\) is the output of \(i\), and the sums run over the tokens up to \(i\), because \(i\) may read only those. For “it” the weighted sum of the four values, with the unrounded weights, is \(0.113\,(0.2, 0.9) + 0.282\,(-0.8, 0.5) + 0.422\,(1.1, -0.2) + 0.183\,(0.3, -0.7) = (0.32, 0.03)\).

Analogy. A Python dictionary (lookup by key in Part 0) returns the value whose key equals the query. Attention returns a blend of the values of the tokens it reads, weighted by how well their keys match.

Where it breaks. A dictionary reports a miss when no key equals the query, but attention never does. Softmax divides by the sum of the \(e^s\), so the weights add up to 1 even when no key matches well. The blend also hides its parts, so the output vector alone does not show which value contributed what.

Quick quiz

Scores 2, 2 and 3 for three keys. What are the weights?

\(e^2 = 7.39\) twice and \(e^3 = 20.09\), which sum to 34.87. The weights are 0.212, 0.212 and 0.576.

The weights are 0.5 and 0.5 and the values are (2, 0) and (0, 4). What is the output?

\(0.5\times(2,0) + 0.5\times(0,4) = (1, 2)\), halfway between the two values.

Reading the figure

Read the figure from left to right. The coral arrow is the query of the chosen token and the navy arrows are the keys. A dot product is large when two arrows point the same way and are long (0.5). The table gives the dot product, the score after dividing by \(\sqrt{2}\), and the softmax weight. The boxes below show the working for the row you click. In the right plane the dotted pieces, a weight times a value, lie end to end and add up to the output arrow. The division by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) is explained in the next section.

A task and a second worked case

To give “young” the largest weight, the query of “it” has to point further up than the key of “young”. When the query points between the two keys, the longer key of “hammerhead” still wins, because length counts as well as direction. For \(\mathbf{q} = (0.8, 0.9)\), which points the same way as the key of “young”, the dot products are 1.45 with “young” and 1.66 with “hammerhead”.

For a second worked case, choose the query of “young”. It can read only “the” and itself, and its query is \((0.4, 0.5)\). The dot products are \(0.4\times0.3 + 0.5\times(-0.5) = -0.13\) and \(0.4\times0.8 + 0.5\times0.9 = 0.77\). Divided by 1.414 these are \(-0.09\) and \(0.54\). Then \(e^{-0.09} = 0.91\) and \(e^{0.54} = 1.72\), which sum to 2.63, so the weights are 35% and 65%. The output is \(0.35\times(0.2, 0.9) + 0.65\times(-0.8, 0.5) = (-0.45, 0.64)\), the same as the figure.

Softmax and the sum of 1

Softmax makes the weights positive and gives them a sum of 1. Only differences between scores matter: adding 5 to all the scores leaves the weights unchanged (0.7).

Symbols

  • \(s_{ij}\) is the score of token \(i\) for token \(j\). \(\mathbf{q}_i\) is the query of token \(i\), \(\mathbf{k}_j\) the key of token \(j\), and \(d_k\) the key size.
  • \(a_{ij}\) is the weight token \(i\) gives to token \(j\): between 0 and 1, and the weights of one \(i\) add up to 1. The sum runs over \(j'\le i\), the tokens that \(i\) may read.
  • \(\mathbf{o}_i\) is the output of token \(i\): a vector with the length of \(\mathbf{v}\). The next chapter adds it to the token's running vector.

In NumPy

The same steps in NumPy, with the numbers of the figure. The code blocks of this page share their variables, so press Run on them from the top.

import numpy as np
# keys and values of: the, young, hammerhead, it
K = np.array([[0.3, -0.5], [0.8, 0.9], [1.4, 0.6], [0.5, 0.4]])
V = np.array([[0.2, 0.9], [-0.8, 0.5], [1.1, -0.2], [0.3, -0.7]])
q = np.array([1.2, 0.5])               # query of "it"
d_k = len(q)

scores = K @ q / np.sqrt(d_k)          # one score per key
w = np.exp(scores - scores.max())
w = w / w.sum()                        # softmax
out = w @ V                            # weighted sum of the values
print("scores ", scores.round(3))
print("weights", w.round(3), w.sum().round(3))
print("output ", out.round(3))
scores  [0.078 0.997 1.4   0.566]
weights [0.113 0.282 0.422 0.183] 1.0
output  [0.316 0.03 ]

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Print the weights of one token and add them up. They must add up to 1 along a row. If the columns add up to 1 instead, softmax ran over the wrong axis (axis=0 where a row needs axis=-1). The output still looks plausible, so this bug is easy to miss.

Why the scores are scaled

Guess first. A query and a key are two lists of 64 independent random numbers with mean 0 and variance 1. Their dot product is a sum of 64 products. About how large is a typical dot product: about 1, about 8 or about 64?

The variance of some numbers is the average squared distance from their mean, and their spread is the square root of the variance (Part 0). For random numbers like those above, a dot product of a query and a key with \(d_k\) numbers has a spread of \(\sqrt{d_k}\). Scaling divides the dot products by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) before softmax, which keeps the spread near 1 for any key size. Scaling matters because a large spread saturates the softmax: one weight is near 1, the others are near 0, and the slopes that training uses are near 0.

  1. The figure draws 300 random queries with 8 random keys for a query, which gives 2,400 dot products. The mean largest weight is the mean, over the 300 queries, of the largest of the 8 softmax weights of a query.
  2. At \(d_k = 64\) with the box ticked, the 2,400 scores (dot products divided by \(\sqrt{d_k}\)) have a spread of 0.98. Untick the box: the 2,400 dot products themselves have a spread of 7.84.
  3. Slide \(d_k\) from 4 to 1,024 with the box unticked: the spread of the dot products grows like \(\sqrt{d_k}\) and the largest weight rises toward 100%. With the box ticked, it stays between 34% and 38%.

At \(d_k = 64\), dividing the dot products by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) lowers their spread from about 8 to about 1 and the mean largest weight from 88% to 36%.

How it works

Take \(d_k = 64\). The dot product is the sum of the 64 products \(q_mk_m\), where \(q_m\) and \(k_m\) are the \(m\)-th numbers of the query and the key. A product of two independent numbers with mean 0 and variance 1 has variance \(1\times1 = 1\). Variances of independent terms add, so the sum has variance 64 and a spread of 8.

64terms in the sum, dk×1variance of one product=64variance of q·k→8spread, √64÷8√dk=1spread after scaling

Why a large spread hurts. Without scaling, two dot products that differ by 8 give weights in the ratio \(e^{8} = 2{,}981\) to 1, so the top key can take almost all the weight. A softmax weight \(p\) has the slope \(p(1-p)\) in its own score, which is 0.001 at \(p = 0.999\). Almost no gradient then flows back through that weight (vanishing gradients), so training would change the queries and keys slowly. Vaswani and others (2017) suspect that this is the reason for the scaling.

Common belief. Scaling forces attention to stay soft.

Why it fails. The spread of 1 follows from assuming random numbers with variance 1, a model of the start of training. Training can make the queries and keys larger, so the attention can sharpen. Head L4H11 of section 5 has scores of size 35 after scaling and puts about 100% of its weight on one token.

Better account. Scaling gives a good starting point, and training can move away from it where that helps.

Quick quiz

With \(d_k = 16\), what are the spread of \(\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k}\) before and after scaling?

Before: \(\sqrt{16} = 4\). After dividing by 4: 1.

With \(d_k = 16\), two dot products differ by 16. What is the ratio of their weights with scaling and without it?

With scaling the scores differ by \(16/\sqrt{16} = 4\), so the ratio is \(e^{4} = 55\) to 1. Without scaling it is \(e^{16} = 8.9\) million to 1.

Reading the figure

Switch the scaling off and slide \(d_k\) up. The histogram widens like \(\sqrt{d_k}\), and the bars on the right turn into a single tall bar. The counting of variances is the same as the one that fixed the weight spread of a layer in B6 (Xavier and He initialisation).

Scores of trained heads

Over the three sentences of the heat map, the scores of head L4H11 that the mask keeps range from −35.2 to 34.1. Those of head L1H10 range from −8.9 to 0.2. The largest sizes are negative scores, found in the sentence “He let it go”.

Symbols

\[ \operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k}) = \sum_{m=1}^{d_k}\operatorname{Var}(q_m k_m) = d_k\cdot 1\cdot 1 = d_k \]

  • \(q_m, k_m\) are the \(m\)-th numbers of the query and the key, assumed independent with mean 0 and variance 1 (the assumption in Vaswani and others, 2017).
  • \(\operatorname{Var}\) is the variance. The first equality follows because the variance of a sum of independent terms is the sum of their variances.

Temperature

Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) is the same as softmax with temperature \(T = \sqrt{d_k}\) (D3), here \(T = 8\).

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Divide by the square root of the key size of one head (64 in GPT-2 small), not of the whole embedding (768). If a model's attention is nearly one-hot from the first step, or its loss turns into NaN, check the scale first. PyTorch's scaled_dot_product_attention applies \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) by default; the NumPy code in this chapter gives the same result (Practice 3).

All tokens at once, and the causal mask

Guess first. While GPT-2 learns from the text “We put it back”, it predicts the next word at all positions in one pass. At the token “it” the next word, “back”, is already in the input. If attention may read it, what would the model learn, and what would happen when it writes a new report?

Stack the queries, keys and values of a text as the rows of matrices \(Q\), \(K\) and \(V\). The product \(QK^{\top}/\sqrt{d_k}\) gives the scores of all pairs of tokens at once, with the scores of token \(i\) in row \(i\). Before softmax, the causal mask replaces the scores above the diagonal, where token \(j\) comes after token \(i\), by \(-\infty\), a value below any number. Since \(e^{-\infty} = 0\), softmax gives later tokens the weight 0. The table of weights is the attention matrix.

  1. Press “1 Scores”, “2 Mask” and “3 Softmax” in turn: the mask hatches the cells above the diagonal, which get weight 0 after softmax. The readout counts the scores kept.
  2. At stage 3 untick “Causal mask”: the same scores would send 69% of a row’s weight, on average, to later tokens. GPT-2 always runs with the mask, so this view shows the weights that the same scores would give without it.

With the mask, any head keeps 210 of the 400 scores of “Tag 4127 twice”; without it, L4H11 would send 69% of a row’s weight, on average, to later tokens.

How it works

Take the query of “hammerhead” in the figure of section 3. It may read three tokens, with the scores 0.099, 0.580 and 0.877, and the later key of “it” gets \(-\infty\). Then \(e^s\) = 1.104, 1.786, 2.403 and 0, which add up to 5.293, so the weights are 0.209, 0.337, 0.454 and 0. For a text of \(n\) tokens the mask keeps \(n(n+1)/2\) of the \(n^2\) scores, 210 of 400 for the 20 tokens of the figure. In the formula below, the matrix \(M\) adds 0 to the scores a token may read and \(-\infty\) to the others.

\[ \mathrm{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\Big(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}} + M\Big)V,\qquad M_{ij} = \begin{cases} 0 & j \le i\\ -\infty & j > i\end{cases} \]

  1. Now the question at the top: what does a model learn when attention may read the next word? We trained two copies of a tiny one-head model on 400 made-up reports, one with the mask and one without. The loss is lower when the predictions are better. The solid lines are the losses on the training reports. At step 400, the end of the slider, the copy without the mask (coral) has 0.06, below the 0.28 of the masked copy (teal).
  2. The dotted lines show the loss on 100 new reports with the mask on, as when the model writes. The copy trained without the mask ends at 2.49 and the masked copy at 0.30. Drag the slider back to step 40: the dotted coral line is at its lowest, 1.28, and rises from there while the solid coral line keeps falling.

Common belief. The mask matters when we generate text, and training can do without it.

Why it fails. In training the whole text is known, so without the mask the token at position \(t\) can read position \(t+1\), which is the label. This is a leak: the answer reaches the input, and the loss falls for the wrong reason. The code under Go deeper includes a leak test.

Better account. The mask makes training match use, because at any position the input contains only what it will contain when the model writes. Encoder models such as BERT drop the mask on purpose and change the task to avoid a leak (model families).

Quick quiz

A text has 6 tokens. How many scores does the causal mask keep, out of how many?

\(6\times7/2 = 21\) of 36.

A model trained without the mask has a far lower training loss than a masked model. Why can it still do worse when it writes a report?

Without the mask a token can read the next word, which is the label, so the low training loss comes from reading the answer. When the model writes, that word does not exist yet, and on new reports with the mask on the loss was 2.49 against 0.30.

Go deeper formula, cost, tiny models, NumPy, mask bugs about 4 min

The formula in one line

Stack the queries as the rows of a matrix \(Q\) with \(n\) rows and \(d_k\) columns, and the keys as the rows of \(K\). Then \(QK^{\top}\) has \(n\) rows and \(n\) columns, and its entry in row \(i\) and column \(j\) is \(\mathbf{q}_i\cdot\mathbf{k}_j\) (0.5). Divide by \(\sqrt{d_k}\), add the mask, run softmax along the rows and multiply by \(V\). That is the formula of the paper in one line, with the mask added.

Symbols

  • \(Q, K, V\) have one row per token: the queries, keys and values. \(M\) is the mask: 0 where a token may read, \(-\infty\) where it may not.
  • Softmax runs along the rows. The result has one output row per token, so all tokens are handled in one pass.

How the cost grows

For GPT-2's full window of 1,024 tokens, the mask keeps 524,800 entries per head, and 75,571,200 over the 144 heads. Doubling the length of a text makes the table four times as large. That is the \(n^2\) growth of 0.2, and D6 returns to it.

What the tiny model learned

Training made the model without the mask put weight on position \(t+1\), which contains the label. Take the roughly 1,500 of 11,715 word positions where the masked model finds the next word hard (loss above 1 nat). There the model without the mask puts 39% of its weight on the next word, which is the answer itself. At generation time that word does not exist yet, so the model has learned a skill it cannot use when it writes.

In NumPy

The first block is the whole of attention for a text, with the mask as an option. Its output for the four-token example matches the figure of section 3, and row 4 is the case worked there. The block uses the variables of the code in section 3, so run that code first.

# queries of the four tokens
Q = np.array([[0.6, -0.2], [0.4, 0.5], [0.8, 0.2], [1.2, 0.5]])

def attention(Q, K, V, causal=True):
    n, d_k = Q.shape
    S = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d_k)             # n x n table of scores
    if causal:
        keep = np.tril(np.ones((n, n), bool))
        S = np.where(keep, S, -np.inf)     # hide the future
    W = np.exp(S - S.max(axis=1, keepdims=True))
    W = W / W.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)   # softmax along the rows
    return W, W @ V

W, out = attention(Q, K, V)
print(W.round(3))
print(out.round(3))
[[1.    0.    0.    0.   ]
 [0.346 0.654 0.    0.   ]
 [0.209 0.337 0.454 0.   ]
 [0.113 0.282 0.422 0.183]]
[[ 0.2    0.9  ]
 [-0.454  0.638]
 [ 0.271  0.266]
 [ 0.316  0.03 ]]

A leak test

Debug tip. Check the mask first. Before anything else, run a leak test: change the last token of an input and compare the outputs at the earlier positions. With a causal mask they must not move at all.

rng = np.random.default_rng(4127)
n, d = 5, 4
X = rng.normal(size=(n, d))
X2 = X.copy()
X2[-1] = rng.normal(size=d)          # change only the last token
for causal in (True, False):
    # tokens serve as queries, keys and values
    _, a = attention(X, X, X, causal)
    _, b = attention(X2, X2, X2, causal)
    name = "mask   " if causal else "no mask"
    change = np.abs(a[:-1] - b[:-1]).max().round(4)
    print(name, "largest change in the earlier rows:", change)
mask    largest change in the earlier rows: 0.0
no mask largest change in the earlier rows: 0.5637

Common mistakes

Other common mask bugs are these. The mask is added after softmax, so the weights no longer add up to 1. The mask is transposed, which hides the past and shows the future. Or a padding mask that hides all the tokens of a row, which gives a row of NaN. Keep at least one visible token per row.

More questions

Row 3 of a masked table of four tokens is 0.209, 0.337, 0.454, 0. Why is the last entry 0, and why do the others still add up to 1?

Token 3 may not read token 4, so its score was set to \(-\infty\) and \(e^{-\infty}=0\). Softmax then runs over the three remaining scores, and those weights add up to 1.

Many heads

Guess first. GPT-2 small has 144 heads: 12 per layer, in 12 layers. Do you expect them all to behave alike, or to differ widely? How would you tell?

A head is one set of matrices \(W_Q\), \(W_K\) and \(W_V\) with the attention they compute. A layer runs \(H\) heads side by side on vectors of \(d_k = d/H\) numbers. Here the model width \(d\) is the number of entries in a token's vector, 768 in GPT-2 small, so \(d_k = 64\). The layer concatenates the outputs of the heads, which joins them end to end, and mixes the result with a learned output matrix \(W_O\).

  1. Squares are the 144 heads, darker for a larger average weight on the first token over seven short texts. The readout counts 29 heads above 80%; hover over L5H5 (row 5, column 5) to read 87%.
  2. Choose “Previous token”: L4H11 (row 4, column 11) is the darkest square (hover to read 100%), and the next one, L2H2, has 55%. Press “Pin the four heads of the sentence view” to compare their attention tables.

The 144 heads differ widely: in these texts 29 put more than 80% of their weight on the first token, and L4H11 puts about 100% on the previous token.

How it works

Count the parameters of the attention part of one GPT-2 small layer. One head has \(3 \times 768 \times 64 = 147{,}456\) parameters, twelve heads have \(12\times147{,}456 = 1{,}769{,}472\), and \(W_O\) adds \(768^2 = 589{,}824\). So the layer has \(1{,}769{,}472 + 589{,}824 = 2{,}359{,}296 = 4\times768^2\) parameters.

12heads, H×64numbers per head, dk=768joined vector, d→768 × 768output matrix WO→768mixed output

Several heads give several blends of the same text. A token may need the previous token and an earlier copy of itself separately, and one head would mix them into a single blend. The cost stays about the same as for one head of 768 numbers (Vaswani and others, 2017), because a head works on shorter vectors.

Common belief. All heads have a clear job, such as “subject”, “noun” or “previous word”.

Why it fails. The grid shows many heads that put most of their weight on the first token. The sharp heads of this chapter are the easy cases, chosen because their patterns are clear. A name only says where the weight fell on a few sentences.

Better account. Heads are learned ways to blend. We described four of them, and the grid does not show what the other 140 do. To say what a head does, test it by changing it (attention maps as explanations).

Quick quiz

A model has width 512 and 8 heads. What is \(d_k\), and how many numbers does the joined vector have?

\(d_k = 512/8 = 64\). The joined vector has \(8\times64 = 512\) numbers, the same as the width.

A head puts 95% of its weight on the first token for most tokens. What does its output look like for those tokens, and how could you find out whether the head matters?

The output is a weighted sum of the values, so it is about 0.95 times the value of the first token plus a small part from the others. This is nearly the same vector for those tokens, so the head adds little that depends on the reading token. A few tokens with other weights, such as the repeated tag in L5H5, may still matter. To find out, remove the head and watch the output.

Go deeper reading the grid, symbols, biases, cost, NumPy about 2 min

Reading the grid

Switch the measure and click squares to pin up to four heads. The tables show lower triangles, as the mask requires. L4H11 gives a bright line just below the diagonal. L0H1 gives a bright diagonal (press “Pin the four heads” to see it). L5H5 gives a bright first column, and a short bright diagonal of three cells near the end, for the repeated Tag 4127. L1H10 gives a soft blur. The names describe where the weights fall on these sentences. We chose these four because their patterns are easy to describe, and the grid does not show what the other heads do.

Symbols

\[ \mathrm{head}_h = \mathrm{Attention}\big(XW_Q^{h},\,XW_K^{h},\,XW_V^{h}\big),\qquad \mathrm{MultiHead}(X) = \big[\mathrm{head}_1;\ \dots;\ \mathrm{head}_H\big]\,W_O \]

  • \(X\) is the matrix with the token vectors as rows (\(n\) rows, \(d\) columns). \(W_Q^{h}, W_K^{h}, W_V^{h}\) are the matrices of head \(h\), all with \(d\) rows and \(d_k\) columns.
  • \(H\) is the number of heads and \(d_k = d/H\). The square brackets with semicolons join the head outputs end to end. \(W_O\) has \(d\) rows and \(d\) columns.

Biases

Parameters are often called weights. They are different from attention weights. GPT-2 adds 3,072 biases to these parameters: \(3\times768\) for the three projections and 768 for \(W_O\). The model width \(d\) is the length of a token's vector, the embedding size of D2, and 768 in GPT-2 small.

Cost

Cost matters for the next chapters. Attention takes about \(n^2 d\) steps per layer (Vaswani and others, 2017, Table 1), so a longer text gets expensive quickly. D5 puts attention inside a transformer block, and D6 deals with long texts.

In NumPy

The block below uses the function attention of the code in section 5, so run that code first.

def multi_head(X, Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo, H):
    n, d = X.shape
    dk = d // H
    heads = []
    for h in range(H):
        sl = slice(h * dk, (h + 1) * dk)   # the columns of head h
        q, k, v = X @ Wq[:, sl], X @ Wk[:, sl], X @ Wv[:, sl]
        heads.append(attention(q, k, v)[1])
    return np.concatenate(heads, axis=1) @ Wo   # join, then mix

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
X = rng.normal(size=(4, 8))
Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo = (rng.normal(0, 0.3, (8, 8)) for _ in range(4))
out = multi_head(X, Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo, H=2)
print(X.shape, "->", out.shape, "with 2 heads of", 8 // 2, "numbers")
print("weights in the four matrices:", 4 * 8 * 8)
(4, 8) -> (4, 8) with 2 heads of 4 numbers
weights in the four matrices: 256

Exercises

Theory

  1. theory A token has the query \(\mathbf{q} = (1, 2)\) and can read three keys, \((2, 0)\), \((0, 1)\) and \((1, 1)\), with \(d_k = 2\). Compute the dot products, the scores and the softmax weights. Which key wins and by how much?

    Hint

    Divide by \(\sqrt2 = 1.414\) before exponentiating.

  2. theory Show that for independent \(q_m, k_m\) with mean 0 and variance 1, the product \(q_mk_m\) has variance 1 and \(\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k}\) has variance \(d_k\). Then use the figure of section 4 to say what happens to the largest weight among 8 keys when \(d_k\) goes from 4 to 256 without scaling, and with scaling.

  3. theory A text has \(n = 6\) tokens. How many entries of the score table does a causal mask keep? Repeat for \(n = 1{,}024\), per head and over 144 heads. Then compare the invented Hindi report m05 (117 GPT-2 tokens, D1) with its English meaning (23 tokens): what is the ratio of kept entries?

  4. theory Count the weights of the attention part of one GPT-2 small layer in two ways. First as \(4\times768^2\). Then as 12 heads of three matrices of 768 by 64, plus \(W_O\). Why are the two counts equal?

Practice

  1. practice Write attention(Q, K, V, causal) in NumPy without looking at the chapter. Test it on the four-token example: all rows must add up to 1 and the entries above the diagonal must be 0. Then write the leak test of section 5 and run it with the mask on and off.

  2. practice Download attention.json. For the four heads and the three sentences, compute the mean weight that a token puts on the previous token. Use tokens 1 to \(n-1\) and the masked weights w. Which head scores highest, and what does it score on sentence s1?

  3. practice Compare your function with torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True) on random inputs of size (1, 1, 6, 16). Report the largest absolute difference. What changes if you drop the \(\sqrt{d_k}\)?

Think deeper

  1. open SharkCam messages repeat tag numbers, for example Tag 4127 in a report and again in a follow-up. Describe how attention could help a model repeat the number the second time. What would you test to check that a given head does this, and what result would count against it?

  2. open A friend says: “The model gave ‘hammerhead’ a weight of 0.42, so that word explains the output.” Design two tests that would show whether the claim is true. What results would make you withdraw it?

    Hint

    Think of changing the input and of switching off a head. See B9.

  3. open A dive log has 2,400 frames at 1 frame per second (the made-up dive log of the SharkCam data). If all frames were tokens, how many entries would one head's causal table contain? Name two ways to cut the cost and say what the two would give up.

Come back later

Try these after two days, and again after a week, without looking back.

Dividing the scores by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) is a softmax temperature. Which \(T\) is it for \(d_k = 64\), and does it make the weights sharper or flatter than without scaling? (Chapter D3)

\(T = 8\). A higher temperature flattens the weights, so scaling makes them flatter than the raw scores would.

In a saturated softmax one weight is 0.999. What is its slope \(p(1-p)\), and why does that matter for training? (Chapter B4)

\(0.999 \times 0.001 \approx 0.001\). A slope this small multiplies the gradient that passes back through the softmax by about a thousandth, so the other keys learn very little.

In D2, “shark” and “whale” had a dot product of 22.27 in 50 numbers. If those vectors were a query and a key with \(d_k = 50\), what is the score? (Chapter D2)

\(22.27/\sqrt{50} = 22.27/7.07 = 3.15\). (A hypothetical case: an actual model makes \(\mathbf{q}\) and \(\mathbf{k}\) with learned matrices.)
